title: How tariffs, fuel and fertilizer costs are squeezing the U.S.'s biggest apple region
summary: Washington's $9 billion industry grows more than 70% of the nation's fresh apples. Farmers are being pressed by high costs, tariffs and a strong dollar that diminishes foreign purchasing power.
text:
How tariffs, fuel and fertilizer costs are squeezing the U.S.'s biggest apple region
Loading...
As Sean Gilbert stepped out of his white GMC pickup, he breathed in the scent of applewood and Columbia Basin dust. Here, just south of Wapato, Wash., one of his 50-acre Gala and Red Delicious apple orchards is ground into huge piles of mulch chips. The wood chipper is the size of a semi-truck and belts out a screeching racket.
He said this ground will lay fallow. It will cost this fifth-generation apple farmer less to leave it unplanted and weedy than to plant another orchard or crop. He scooped up a handful of applewood mulch. "It's a bit of a relief that we're not going to continue to be hemorrhaging dollars on orchards that the market doesn't want," he said. "It hasn't been making sense for a while."
Washington's $9 billion industry grows nearly 70% of the nation's fresh apples, according to Jon DeVaney, president of the Washington State Tree Fruit Association.
DeVaney said farmers are being pressed by the costs of labor, fuel, fertilizer, equipment, as well as weak exports from international tariffs and a strong dollar that diminishes foreign purchasing power.
He estimated thousands of acres of apple orchards across the Northwest are being rapidly torn out, or are not being actively cared for, because many farmers aren't making money growing the fruit. And after several years of similar economic conditions, many farms have gone deep into debt – with even some large, well-established operations filing for bankruptcy.
Loading...
In the late summer and fall, unpicked apples have been left to rot in branches and on the ground. Over the past few years, an estimated thousands of acres have only been partially picked or not picked at all, according to Kate Tynan, senior vice president of the Northwest Horticultural Council, a trade association that advocates for the Northwest tree fruit industry on federal policy issues and international trade.
Recent federal regulatory changes would effectively lower wages for some immigrant workers and take housing costs out of their paychecks. Tynan said with updates to the way wages are calculated, farm owners are hoping they'll be able to break even – but the farm workers union has pushed back on these changes and an upcoming federal judicial decision could put operators on the hook for backpay for the 2026 season.
U.S. farmers have also been especially hard hit by tariffs and high input costs. The Trump administration announced $12 billion in payments to farmers at the end of 2025 that primarily targeted farmers who grow crops such as soybeans and corn. Tynan said much of that relief has not reached farmers that grow specialty crops like fruit and vegetables.
"The Pacific Northwest has lost an unprecedented number of tree fruit farms in recent years," Tynan said. "Economic conditions have worsened drastically since then, so we know that number is far higher today."

title: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
summary: The verdict follows a months-long trial in New York.
text:
Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
- Published
Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark trial in the US, AP reports.
In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.
Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.
In a statement, Huawei said the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis and vindicates our consistent position over the past eight years".
Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019.
During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms ensure it had a competitive edge.
However, defence attorney Brian Heberlig said Huawei had grown into business with operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff through hard work.

title: The U.S. government is investigating Iranian ties to as many as 50 hacked commercial vessels
summary: The attacks, if officials who spoke to NPR are correct, may be the latest example of Iranian cyberattacks against global critical infrastructure during the war with the U.S.
text:
The U.S. government is investigating Iranian ties to as many as 50 hacked commercial vessels
The U.S. government has intelligence suggesting that up to 50 commercial shipping vessels were recently compromised by cyberattacks, activity federal officials are investigating as potentially linked to Iran.
That's according to a U.S. official familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak on the record, a former military cyber operator and an industry executive briefed on the attacks. The series of breaches was first reported by the The Wall Street Journal.
The attacks against the maritime sector, if officials' suspicions are correct, may be the latest example of Iranian cyberattacks against global critical infrastructure during the ongoing war with the United States.
NPR has reported that cybersecurity experts and U.S. officials believe Iranian hackers were responsible for a series of digital attacks against U.S. water treatment systems across the country in August as well as a pattern of attacks targeting refrigeration cooling systems that led to spoiled food at grocery stores on U.S. military bases and all across Europe as recently as early November.
The Coast Guard and the FBI first partnered in August to send a "highly specialized team" to board two different foreign commercial vessels "in the Gulf of America" heading to U.S. ports, according to a statement provided by the FBI and the Coast Guard. "The captain, crew, and shore-side corporate staff were critical partners in helping to ensure the threats were mitigated," according to the statement.
The FBI and Coast Guard press offices also told NPR that there are no current "reports of operational disruptions, vessel instability, physical danger to crews, or environmental impacts."
However, there are dozens more ships in international waters that the U.S. government believes have been compromised by hackers and many others who might be vulnerable to similar attacks.
According to the U.S. official familiar with the investigation, bad actors took advantage of known vulnerabilities in Fortinet FortiGate devices, which are frequently used in the maritime industry. The Coast Guard and FBI released a cyber bulletin in September warning the industry that bad actors were breaking into these devices, which help manage firewalls and virtual private networks. "Threat actors routinely scan for specific, unpatched vulnerabilities to gain a foothold," the bulletin read.
According to the U.S. official, in some cases, employees aboard the ships suspected something nefarious was going on when they noticed email disruptions or couldn't log in to their accounts, or, in at least one case, an extended communications blackout. The U.S. official declined to comment on how the U.S. government knows about the extent of breaches across the sector.

title: DR Congo says military aircraft missing as rebels claim to shoot down plane
summary: A South African fighter pilot and a Ugandan officer are reportedly among those aboard the downed plane.
text:
DR Congo says military aircraft missing as rebels claim to shoot down plane
- Published
The Democratic Republic of Congo military says it is searching for one of its aircraft, after rebels said they had shot down a warplane in the east.
The military said it had lost contact with a small Cessna 208 cargo plane on Sunday following "poor weather conditions". The fate of the plane and its crew remained uncertain, it added.
On the same day, the rebel Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) said it had shot down a plane of the same type that was on a mission to bomb Minembwe in South Kivu province.
Four people were reportedly on board, including a Ugandan and a South African pilot, who is said to have been captured alive.
On Tuesday, the FRN said the plane they had shot down was a Cessna 208, which had been "converted into a light attack aircraft" enabling it "to carry and launch precision-guided bombs and missiles".
Its wreckage now lies 10km (6 miles) from Minembwe, a rebel statement said, adding that a Ugandan and South African "mercenaries" had been captured.
The BBC has not independently verified the rebel claim, or whether the aircraft reported missing by the DR Congo military is the same one the rebels say they shot down.
South Africa's government has not commented, while Uganda's military has denied any involvement.

A statement attributed to army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba posted on X said: "UPDF had nothing to do with the aircraft that was shot down in Minembwe. We have penalized that company."
The statement did not identify the company or explain what penalty had been imposed.
Gen Kainerugaba later posted that "no Ugandan is allowed to work for mercenary companies in [DR Congo]".
Uganda's denial followed the circulation of a video apparently showing a man being questioned beside the plane's wreckage.
In the footage, the man identifies himself as Ugandan and claims he had been sent by the government. The BBC has not independently verified the video or established the man's identity.
He and the alleged South African pilot are said to be the only other survivors.
South African media outlet Mail & Guardian quoted an FRN spokesperson identifying the pilot as a South African and a "mercenary [who] has no link to the place that he was hired to destroy".
"Unfortunately, we have a multi-country conflict in the eastern DRC," deputy FRN spokesperson Oscar Balinda told the outlet.
In 2022, DR Congo's army blamed M23 rebels, who are now part of the FRN, of shooting down a UN helicopter in which eight people died. The rebels denied it.
The Congolese government has in the past used foreign mercenaries to fight the rebels.
In recent days, fighting between the FRN and the government has intensified with the rebel group accusing the government of targeting heavily populated areas.

title: US court unseals heavily redacted records on Ilhan Omar home search
summary: Prosecutors say they are pursuing evidence of crimes allegedly committed by the Democratic congresswoman over decades, and unrelated to her work in Congress.
text:
US court unseals heavily redacted records on Ilhan Omar home search
- Published
A federal court has unsealed heavily redacted documents related to the search of US lawmaker Ilhan Omar's home last month, despite an attempt from prosecutors to block the release.
Some 169 pages of court documents show investigators were looking for potential criminal violations involving Omar going all the way back to 1980.
The Minnesota Democrat, who has not been charged with a crime and has denied any wrongdoing, moved to the US from Somalia in 1995 and became a naturalised citizen in 2000.
Omar, who has been an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, described the search on social media as "an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement".
After the search of her home in October, immigration agents offered limited details saying it was related to an ongoing federal criminal investigation.
The exchanges in the released court documents show a back-and-forth between a judge and federal prosecutors over executing a warrant and releasing the documents to the public.
Although heavily redacted, the documents offer a glimpse into what the investigation may involve.
The records show the government applied for a warrant to search her Washington DC home for evidence of crimes "involving Ilhan Nur Said Elmi a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar, and occurring between 1980 to the present". The specific offences are redacted in the unsealed documents.
Prosecutors said they were pursuing evidence of crimes that allegedly happened decades ago and do not have anything to do with Omar's work in Congress.
Omar's immigration records have been scrutinised in the past by Republicans and earlier this year, a fellow congresswoman, Nancy Mace of South Carolina, unsuccessfully sought a subpoena for her records.
In September, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told a conservative podcaster "something is going to happen", and made allegations of marital fraud against Omar.
Separately, the White House's border tsar, Tom Homan, told Fox News that Omar was being investigated for unspecified immigration violations.
Omar denied the allegations.
"I will say it again so it's as clear as possible: I'm not at all worried about these investigations, because they are complete shams," she said.
Last month, Trump referred to the search of Omar's home, saying: "I don't know what they're doing with it, but I can tell you this: she's a disaster."
The timing of the raid - 22 days before the November midterm elections - raised concerns from Omar's fellow Democrats.
The justice department has a longstanding policy of refraining from most enforcement action that is "likely to raise an issue or the perception" it is being brought for the purpose of affecting any election or to disadvantage a candidate.

title: Who really owns the Albanian land Jared Kushner wants to turn into a 5-star resort?
summary: Albania's Prime Minister Edi Rama has vowed that Kushner's resort project will go ahead as planned. But an ongoing investigation by Albania's state prosecutor into forged land titles could halt the project.
text:
Who really owns the Albanian land Jared Kushner wants to turn into a 5-star resort?
ZVERNEC, Albania — In the summer of 2021, Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump boarded a yacht owned by Nat Rothschild, an heir to the European banking family. On the way from Montenegro to Greece, the yacht anchored off the coast of Albania.
And, as Kushner told an investment conference last year, that's when Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama arrived at the boat to tell them about his plan for the country.
"I was very impressed by what he wanted to do with the country," said Kushner. "I really didn't know anything about the country and I didn't understand the history, and the darkness of the history with the communism and terrible leadership led to it being fully undeveloped as a nation."
A year later, Kushner was looking for development opportunities in the Balkans. He returned to the Albanian coast — to the city of Vlore, which was finishing the construction of an airport atop a wetland near an undeveloped coastline. "And obviously, a country's going to build an airport by the coast in a place they think is most beautiful," Kushner told the conference, "so we went there and we were looking for opportunities, and we found some incredible opportunities."
Kushner found those opportunities at Hidrovor Beach, an expanse of caramel-colored sand along the southern Albanian coast, with the gentle waves of the Adriatic lapping its perimeter and a view of an uninhabited island. A company working for Kushner purchased this land and 300 acres surrounding it for more than $130 million in April. But several people here tell NPR this is not Kushner's land.
They say it's theirs.
Land grabs and falsified documents
"This land here belonged to my family for centuries," says Gentian Mocka, who claims his family has owned this strip of beach and wetland since the time of the Ottoman Empire. He provided NPR land titles that appear to prove this.
After World War II, Albania's Communist government seized it — along with all private land.
When communism fell in 1991, families like Mocka's embarked on a years-long process to get their land back. "But then our problems started with the guys that were much more powerful than we were — had a lot of political support, were very rich and very well connected with the politics of that time," says Mocka.
In 2005, Mocka learned that someone else was laying claim to his family's land — a fellow Albanian named Artur Shehu. It was a familiar name for those who lived here in the 1990s, when the regional capital of Vlore was outside the control of the country's government. It was instead run by mafia-style gangs. At the time, Shehu was well-known to police in Vlore for his alleged involvement in a crime syndicate that, according to Albanian prosecutors, smuggled drugs and migrants into Europe. He fled Albania in 1999, after what police say was a shootout with a rival gang.

title: Nigerian monarch, 92, suspended after sexual assault claims
summary: The Emir of Daura is one of Nigeria's best-known monarchs, with politicians often trying to gain his support.
text:
Nigerian monarch, 92, suspended after sexual assault claims
- Published
One of Nigeria's best-known monarchs, the Emir of Daura, has been suspended from all official engagements and travel following allegations of sexual assault by a Polish tourist.
The visitor said Umar Farouk Umar, 92, had grabbed her chest during a tourism encounter and that she felt disgusted by the experience.
The allegation sparked widespread discussion across social media platforms, with many calling for the suspension of the emir and an investigation - calls the Katsina state government has now heeded.
Umar has not commented on the allegations or his suspension.
He is one of several emirs - a traditional role dating back to pre-colonial times - who still wield great cultural and religious influence in northern Nigeria, although they have lost their political power.
Daura, where Umar serves as emir, holds an extremely important position for the Hausa people who dominate northern Nigeria. It is widely regarded as their spiritual homeland and the origin of the Hausa royal lineage, serving as the core of Hausa origin mythology and the legitimate foundation of traditional authority.
Politicians routinely visit his palace for royal prayers and to gain his support.
On her Instagram page, the tourist said she had spent 30 days travelling around Nigeria before visiting the Emir's palace on 14 November.
She posted a video, which has since been deleted, in which a man who appears to be the emir is holding her hands in his lap.
After some moments she was heard saying: "Stop, stop" as the hands reached for her chest.
According to a statement, Katsina Governor Dikko Umaru Radda directed the immediate constitution of a committee to investigate the allegations.
The statement said the state government was taking the allegations seriously and would rely on the committee's findings to determine the appropriate course of action.
It said the committee's findings and recommendations would be fully implemented, stressing that justice would be served.
However, it did not disclose the membership of the investigative committee, its terms of reference or the timeline for submitting its report.
The emir has been on the throne since 2007, succeeding his brother Bashar dan Umaru, who reigned for 41 years.

title: US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
summary: Nvidia's share price have fallen 7% as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's reinstatement.
text:
US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
- Published
US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.
Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.
Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Asked several times on Tuesday if the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."
Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged China spy who led Megaspeed, a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.
The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping to divert advanced chips to China.
In a joint statement last week, the commerce and justice departments said they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".
But speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Blanche said the latter department has "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.
"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.
Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with any efforts to get to the bottom of whether the company or Huang potentially knew about any chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.
"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people.
"It shouldn't be what my message would be either."
While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.
The company's share price was down more than 7% in early afternoon trading, but remained well above the level it closed at on Friday, before Huang's return was announced.

title: Storms targeting both US coasts threaten to snarl Thanksgiving travel for millions
summary: Two storms, including a major Nor'easter on the east coast, are expected to impact millions of people celebrating the holiday with family and friends.
text:
Storms targeting both US coasts threaten to snarl Thanksgiving travel for millions
- Published
Stormy weather on both US coasts could disrupt travel for millions over the Thanksgiving period.
The American Automobile Association (AAA) predicts 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles from home for Thanksgiving between Tuesday 24 November and Monday 30 November.
The US National Weather Service says a series of Pacific storm systems will bring widespread rain, mountain snow, gusty winds and high surf to the West Coast this week, with coastal flood watches widely in place.
Meanwhile, Wednesday will see a storm off the south-east coast intensify and run north along the eastern seaboard. This will develop into a powerful Nor'easter storm over Thanksgiving, bringing floods, strong winds and heavy rain.
West Coast flood risk
The West Coast will be badly affected in the run up to Thanksgiving, with a strong Pacific storm expected to move into the north-west on Tuesday night and affect the area throughout Wednesday.
The storm will bring particularly heavy rain because it will tap into an atmospheric river, a huge, invisible ribbon of water vapour.
Impacts will include strong winds, heavy rain at lower elevations and snow in the mountains from western Washington to Northern California.
The AAA predicts the vast majority of holiday travellers, 72.9 million, will travel by car.
Drivers could see significant delays along I-5 between Seattle and Sacramento as a result of the storm. Mountain travel could also be affected on the I-80 and I-90.
The heaviest rain is expected to miss Los Angeles and much of Southern California.
With the full Beaver moon on Tuesday, the West Coast is also expecting the highest tides of the year, coupled with the incoming storm. A coastal flood advisory is in place for the Pacific Northwest and parts of California.
The worst rain is expected to come late Wednesday into Thursday, with another storm forecast for Friday evening.
The San Francisco mayor has warned that the city is bracing for significant weather impacts in the coming days.
Daniel Lurie urged Bay Area residents to check the weather forecast before travelling and avoid unnecessary journeys.

title: What should it cost to insure a home in wildfire country?
summary: Some California homeowners have spent thousands making their homes safer from wildfires. Yet all that work has barely made a dent in their insurance bills. Should they be getting a bigger break?
text:
What should it cost to insure a home in wildfire country?
As a homeowner in rural Northern California, I've lost a lot of sleep worrying about fires. It's not just that big, destructive ones are becoming more common. It's that finding affordable and reliable home insurance has become a nightmare. Without it, the most valuable asset I own could literally go up in smoke. And we've been stuck in a broken insurance market, hoping someone or something can fix it.
Which is why I was so gripped by Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi's recent two-part series on our Planet Money podcast. And it's left me thinking about the economics of making our communities safer. Insurers are spending money to figure out how to keep houses from burning down. Yet some California homeowners tell him they're investing heavily to make their homes and communities safer, and all that work has barely made a dent in their insurance bills.
In the first episode, Alexi goes to a destruction lab in South Carolina where researchers use "crash-test dummies for houses" — the type of wonderful turn of phrase that we love Alexi for — to figure out what actually works to help homes survive climate disasters. They literally light mock houses on fire and subject them to hail and hurricane-force winds to see what happens to them.
Who pays for this lab? Some of the world's biggest insurance companies. They want to know how risky homes are to insure and which building designs will limit damage and shrink the payouts they have to make if disasters strike. It's a pretty wild way to tackle an increasingly urgent question: can we make homes that can better withstand fires and other disasters?
Alexi touches on this in the pod, but insurers have been running experiments like these for more than a century. Back in the early 20th century, scientists at an insurer-funded organization called Underwriters Laboratories tested out new kinds of electrical wiring and consumer appliances to try to reduce the risk of costly fires and electrical accidents. An outfit called the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety does something similar for cars, using crash tests to push for safer auto designs.
Fighting moral hazard in fire country
The insurance industry is way more interesting than most people give it credit for. Part of the magic is obvious. It can insulate us from financial devastation. But there can also be magic in how insurers figure out how big risks really are and what it takes to reduce them. That destruction lab in South Carolina is an amazing example of that.
But Alexi's reporting has me wondering whether insurers could do more to reduce risk. It has to do with this weird thing about insurance. If someone else picks up the tab when something goes wrong, you may have less reason to do everything you can to make sure that it doesn't go wrong in the first place. Economists call this "moral hazard." It's the idea that insurance can reduce incentives to mitigate risk.

title: Indian government has 'lost the plot', says 'cockroach' leader barred from UK flight
summary: Saurav Das says immigration authorities at Delhi airport told him his passport had been flagged.
text:
Indian government has 'lost the plot', says 'cockroach' leader barred from UK flight
- Published
One of the leaders of India's "cockroach" movement has said the Delhi government has "completely lost the plot" after he was stopped from leaving the country for the UK.
Saurav Das said he was meant to board a flight on Tuesday morning but was told by immigration officers his passport had been "flagged" because of discrepancies involving his date of birth.
In an interview with the BBC, Das said there were no discrepancies in his documents, accusing the Indian government of using cheap tactics to stop activists from travelling and speaking on issues that matter to young people.
The BBC has reached out to the federal home ministry, Delhi police and airport officials for comment.
Saurav told the BBC World Service's Newshour programme the incident showed the government was "scared".
"They are scared of the cockroach movement. They're scared of young people asking them questions because they have never had to deal with a generation that wants to ask questions so head on. So that jitters them."
By not allowing him to travel, he said the government had lowered India's stature in the world.
"It's international news that I am unable to travel to the UK," he said. "And this shows Prime Minister Modi in such poor light.
"It's a way to harass, to target activists, young voices in India by the Modi government."
Das said he had been invited by the Oxford Union, as well as universities including Cambridge and Edinburgh, to speak about the movement.
Ratna Singh, another leader of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), wrote: "The manner in which Saurav was not allowed to board today raises deeply troubling questions about the state of freedom of expression and the space being allowed for young voices in this country."
On Tuesday, the London School of Economics Student Union's Amnesty International Unit, a student-led charity group, shared a post on Instagram saying that an event featuring Das had been "indefinitely postponed".
Das, a former journalist, became one of the faces of the CJP - a Gen Z-led movement that began as satire but has since emerged as a youth-led pressure group.
In July, protests spearheaded by the CJP over exam paper leaks led to the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan .
In October, CJP leaders including Das were among thousands detained by the police for trying to hold protests demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Kumar and the Election Commission have denied wrongdoing.
The same month, Das and Ashutosh Ranka, another CJP leader, were jailed for seven days after being arrested for trespassing at a banned protest site in Delhi.
Das insisted the CJP would continue protesting, but it did not want to be a political party "as of today".

title: Trump faces backlash after saying he 'convinced' Nvidia to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang
summary: Nvidia had come under pressure from President Trump to reappoint Huang, whose comeback helped add $1tn to the company's stock value.
text:
Trump faces backlash after saying he 'convinced' Nvidia to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang
- Published
Jensen Huang has been reinstated as the boss of Nvidia less than two weeks after he was forced to resign following the revelations of extra marital affairs, one of which was with a suspected Chinese spy.
The AI chipmaker handed its co-founder his job back, despite rejecting his initial offer to return, after pressure from US President Donald Trump.
Trump said he "made the deal" with the tech giant's board to get Huang his job back, but both the president and Nvidia are facing backlash from lawmakers.
But his comeback added almost $1 trillion to Nvidia's market value as its share price jumped 31%, ending ended a streak of losses on the US stock market.
Nvidia's gains helped boost shares in other tech companies and financial markets in Asia while European markets were flat.
However, despite Huang's return, Nvidia's share price remains down over the past month amid investor concerns about the wider AI industry and future development.
But it is a dramatic return for the man dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech" to the company at the centre of the AI spending boom.
Attention will soon turn to Huang's appearance before Congress next week, where the Nvidia boss will be questioned over his relationship with Alice Huang, alleged to be a spy for China, due to national security concerns.
On Monday, the US Commerce Department announced it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang (no relation) was chief executive. China has denied the spying allegations.
Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's reinstatement after originally resigning on 12 November was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
Last Tuesday, the board explicitly said it did not intend to reinstate him following calls to do so and Huang himself stating he would be open to returning.
The U-turn suggests Nvidia's board believe Huang is irreplaceable.
The 63-year-old, who co-founded the company in 1993, transformed it from a chipmaker for video and computer games to the semiconductor powerhouse it is today, making the chips used in AI systems.
It is now one the most valuable firms in the world. Some believed Huang's departure risked not only the future of Nvidia, but the wider AI industry given the position the company, under Huang, has in the financing of other tech firms.
In a interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump said he had spoken to Nvidia's board of directors and convinced them to bring back Huang.
"They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump said. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot."
"People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it's a threat to lose him," the president added.

title: Doctors struggle to save babies after parents refuse vitamin K
summary: Doctors are fighting an uphill battle against disinformation about routine vitamin K shots given to newborns in the hospital. It helps prevent a rare but devastating bleeding disorder.
text:
Doctors struggle to save babies after parents refuse vitamin K
Every time Torrie LeBlanc failed to persuade a parent to give their baby a vitamin K injection, she thought about the blood-soaked diaper.
It belonged to a newborn delivered last year, in the bustling labor and delivery unit where LeBlanc worked as a physician at the Corewell Health hospital system in Grand Rapids, Mich.
In the early hours the day after the baby girl was born, she suddenly started bleeding "from everywhere," LeBlanc recalled. Her eyes, nose, and rectum all suddenly oozed blood.
The girl's parents cried out for help from their hospital room. Nurses and doctors on the overnight shift rushed her to the neonatal intensive care unit, where they pumped fresh frozen plasma and other blood products into her small body, trying to replace what she was rapidly losing.
Her parents had declined a vitamin K injection for their baby, which is given to most newborns within six hours of birth to prevent rare but life-threatening hemorrhaging. With their baby on the verge of bleeding to death roughly 36 hours after birth, the parents agreed to let doctors administer vitamin K.
It worked. The baby survived, largely because she received treatment almost instantly, according to LeBlanc and an attending physician who helped care for the baby. Had the baby been at home when she started bleeding, they believe she would have died.
What LeBlanc witnessed has become much more common in recent years as more parents, influenced by the anti-vaccine movement and broader mistrust of the medical system, refuse to allow doctors to give their babies vitamin K shots at birth.
Nationally, the rate of newborns who do not receive intramuscular vitamin K has more than doubled, rising from 3.1% of newborns in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025, according to research published in JAMA in November.
The spike moved LeBlanc, a pediatrician, and her colleagues to launch an initiative to reduce the rising number of vitamin K refusals at this hospital. On average, at least one family here refuses the injection for their newborn every day.
Two years in, the team won a modest victory: Vitamin K refusal rates are now flat at the hospital, even as refusals of other standard newborn medications, including the hepatitis B vaccine, continue to climb.
Still, doctors at the hospital say parents now regularly argue against everything from the once-routine vitamin shot to antibiotics for a critically ill infant.
"I honestly thought it would be easier," LeBlanc said, sitting by a sunlit window near the end of a 10-hour shift. "The more people I talk to, the more I learn about the misinformation that's online and the different reasons that people are refusing."
She paused. "It's a work in progress."

title: Zimbabwean convicted in South Africa of trying to fight in Ukraine
summary: Hundreds of people from different African countries have been recruited to fight for Russia, according to Ukraine.
text:
Zimbabwean convicted in South Africa of trying to fight in Ukraine
- Published
A Zimbabwean national has been convicted by a court in South Africa of planning to go to fight in Ukraine.
The country has strict laws which restrict unauthorised involvement in overseas wars.
Twenty-four-year-old Wesley Sothole, who pleaded guilty, was handed a five-year suspended prison sentence and was ordered to be deported from South Africa.
He is one of five Zimbabweans who were arrested at OR Tambo Airport in Johannesburg on 8 November. South African prosecutors have not confirmed which side the Zimbabweans allegedly intended to fight for.
Sothole's four co-accused have yet to enter pleas and are due to return to the Kempton Park Magistrates' Court on 1 December for further plea and sentencing proceedings.
Another four Zimbabweans were arrested at a hotel in Johannesburg at the same time in a joint operation and are facing a different court process.
The investigation has involved South African police, Interpol and other international law enforcement agencies.
South Africa's Foreign Military Assistance Act was passed in 1998 at a time when the government was concerned about members of the former apartheid security services going to fight elsewhere in Africa.
There has been growing concern across Africa over the recruitment of its citizens to fight in the war in Ukraine, with some reportedly being lured to Russia by promises of lucrative civilian employment.
A Ukrainian intelligence assessment estimated earlier this year that more than 1,700 people from 36 countries in Africa have been recruited to fight for Russia.
Some have been captured and are being held as prisoners of war.
In March, Kenya estimated that 252 of its citizens had been illegally conscripted in Russia.
Kenyan Foreign Minister Musalia Mudavadi visited Moscow to address the issue. He said an agreement had been reached for Russia to stop recruiting Kenyan nationals.
In the same month, Zimbabwe said that 15 of its nationals had been killed after being recruited to fight for Russia in Ukraine, with more than 60 still trapped on the frontlines.
The previous month, South Africa secured the return of 17 of its nationals who were allegedly tricked into joining the war.
In December last year, South African authorities arrested five people, including a journalist, for allegedly recruiting people to join the war.
South Africa's government said it condemned "the exploitation of young vulnerable people by individuals working with foreign military entities".
Ukraine has also been recruiting foreign nationals, including from Africa.
Additional reporting by Khanyisile Ngcobo in Johannesburg.

title: US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal
summary: Megaspeed has been accused of funneling AI chips to China after a former executive's affair with Jensen Huang became public.
text:
US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal
- Published
The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America.
The Department of Commerce announced it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US.
The company is mainly a developer of data centres, but in recent weeks a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as a spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang.
The relationship led to additional scrutiny by US officials and heightened concern that Megaspeed was funnelling Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips to China.
When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the commerce department announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed.
Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had an affair with Jensen Huang.
Alice Huang (no relation) was thought by US intelligence to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US.
China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.
On 12 November, Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had had another affair, this one with a Nvidia employee.
On Monday, Nvidia's board reinstated him after US President Donald Trump said he had "convinced" the company and "made the deal".
The commerce department has said it had been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years.
The department said it had suspected the company was violating US export controls by helping to get Nvidia's chips into the hands of companies within China.
China has been blocked from buying such technology since 2022.
Although based in Singapore, Megaspeed has significant business dealings in China.
Alibaba, for instance, the major Chinese online retailer, has been reported to be one if its largest customers.
Megaspeed was a known buyer of billions of dollars of Nvidia computer chips, including through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, which has also been added to the Commerce blacklist.
Nvidia's computer chips, originally designed for use in gaming consols, in recent years have become crucial to the continued growth of the AI industry.
Without enough supply or access to computer chips that are capable of processing the huge amount of data needed to make things like AI chatbots and models run, AI companies will not be able to meet or grow demand from people using AI tools.
That has driven up the value of Nvidia on the stock market, as well as its influence in the AI industry and the White House.

title: They attended Trump's meme coin dinner. It didn't go well
summary: Trump's meme coin dinners have sparked intense controversy. These two guests attended his latest on Sunday — and agreed to provide NPR inside access.
text:
They attended Trump's meme coin dinner. It didn't go well
Headed to what some have called "the most exclusive dinner in the world," hosted by President Trump, crypto investor Morten Christensen and his young sister Gabriëlle Felen had butterflies in their stomachs.
The dinner on Sunday, Nov. 22, was meant to reward the top holders of the president's meme coin — a type of crypto currency that Trump had launched just days before his inauguration.
"I'm excited!," said Christensen. "It's always nice to dress up for an event. My sister looks amazing!"
Christensen — the founder of a crypto website called Airdrop Alert — is a veteran trader who got the crypto bug as far back as 2013. He has attended each of the previous two events Trump has held for the top holders of his meme coin.
For him it was just a chance to get a glimpse of the president. Christensen said that he's not political — and always advises others to "never buy a political meme coin ever."
The events have been intensely controversial. Anti-corruption activists have said they pose enormous conflicts of interest concerns, effectively rewarding those who buy the most coins with access to the president. Top buyers get the closest access.
Christensen was unsure if he would attend this latest dinner. But a sharp drop in the value of Trump's meme coin — from a peak of over $70 in January 2025 to now less than a dollar — had sharply reduced the cost of qualifying as a top holder, which provides access to the dinner.
And, above all, it was a chance to bring his sister Felen for the ride.
On Sunday night, Christensen and Felen agreed to provide NPR with voice memos through an event that turned out to be something they likely won't forget.
Disappointments begin early in the evening
Their butterflies started in the Uber ride to the Trump National Golf Club in Potomac Falls, Virginia. They wanted to head there early. By the time they cleared security, the large room was still filling in.
One of the first things Felen — a recent college graduate — saw was the gift boxes: They contained perfumes, a watch — and a small golden statue of President Trump.
"Pretty nice, pretty nice," said an excited Felen.
The excitement was short-lived.
Christensen bought enough meme coins to qualify as a VIP guest — but when he tried to access the area reserved for the top guests he was denied entry. He was told his name was not on the list.
"Apparently I got removed from the VIP list and I don't know," Christensen said, adding he had even gotten email confirmation.
"But I'm still at the event, so it's all good. It's just a shame."
Many guests appeared to be foreign
Perhaps the most controversial aspect of Trump's meme coin dinners is that many of the top buyers of the meme coin were believed to have been foreign citizens — raising concerns they could be trying to court influence with the president.

title: French ex-President Sarkozy and wife Carla Bruni to face trial
summary: It is the latest case involving Nicolas Sarkozy who became the first French ex-president to go to jail last year.
text:
French ex-President Sarkozy and wife Carla Bruni to face trial
- Published
Nicolas Sarkozy and his wife Carla Bruni-Sarkozy are to face trial next year over charges stemming from the former French president's conviction for conspiring to fund his election campaign with money from late Libyan dictator Muammar Gaddafi.
The charges centre on the retraction of the testimony of a key witness who had initially said he had evidence that could incriminate Sarkozy.
The pair deny any wrongdoing.
Sarkozy was given a five-year sentence in the case last September and became the first French ex-president to go to jail, even though he only spent 20 days behind bars. He has always denied doing anything wrong in the case and the appeals verdict is expected next Monday.
Since losing his re-election bid in 2012, Sarkozy has faced several criminal investigations.
In 2024, he was handed a one-year sentence – of which six months were suspended – over the illegal financing of his 2012 re-election campaign.
In 2021, he was found guilty of trying to bribe a judge and sentenced to three years in jail – two of them suspended – and thus became the first former French president to get a custodial sentence. He was allowed to serve his time at home wearing a tag instead of going to jail.
The new case centres on a Libyan businessman, Ziad Takieddine, who had said he had written proof that Sarkozy's 2007 campaign bid was "abundantly" financed by Tripoli, and that the €50m (£43m) in payments continued after he became president.
Takieddine, who died last year, withdrew his accusations in an interview in 2020.
At the time, Sarkozy was said to have stated: the "truth is finally coming out", but officials found the retraction to be "insincere" and a new investigation was launched into the "Save Sarko" file – the nickname the alleged perpetrators had used for the operation, according to French media.
So the former head of state and his wife, an Italian-born former supermodel and singer, will now face charges of "criminal conspiracy with intent to commit fraud" and benefiting from witness tampering. They deny any wrongdoing.

title: California Democrat to resign from Congress after evidence of sexual misconduct
summary: Jimmy Gomez, who lost his election this month and only serving in the House until the year's end, was accused of sexual misconduct with a staff member.
text:
California Democrat to resign from Congress after evidence of sexual misconduct
- Published
US Representative Jimmy Gomez has said he will resign from Congress after an ethics committee said it found credible evidence that he engaged in sexual misconduct, according to CBS News.
A report released on Monday by the House Ethics Committee stated that Gomez, a California Democrat, made "unwelcome sexual advances" towards a House staff member, "disregarding the power imbalance" between them.
Gomez, 51, said he disagreed with the report's findings but would resign on 1 December. The five-term congressman lost his seat representing part of Los Angeles in the midterm elections this month and was set to leave the House at the end of the year.
The BBC has contacted Gomez's office for comment.
Gomez said in a statement on Monday that he had "strong disagreements" with the committee's findings, but that he saw "no other alternative than to resign", according to CBS, the BBC's US media partner.
He added: "I recognize the seriousness of the Ethics Committee's report and as I previously stated I take full responsibility for the personal mistakes I committed outside of my marriage."
The panel originally investigated a report that Gomez had been seen kissing a younger staffer at a party hosted by then-Congressman Eric Swalwell. That report came shortly after Swalwell, also a California Democrat, resigned over sexual misconduct allegations of his own.
The bipartisan committee announced its investigation into Gomez, who is married, in August, after lawyers for the House staffer accused him of inappropriate sexual contact. He had maintained at the time that while he had made mistakes, his actions were consensual.
The ethics committee interviewed a woman, referred to only as "Witness 1" in the report, who said the congressman made unwanted sexual advances toward her on two occasions, once in public and once in his congressional office, while she was a House staffer.
She alleged Gomez "put his hand down my skirt" while they were at a bar in Washington DC in February 2024, describing the incident as "nonconsensual whatsoever".
Gomez's conduct caused the House staffer "significant and ongoing distress", contributing to her decision to leave her job, according to the report.
The woman's attorneys, Lisa Banks and Sarah Nesbitt, said in a statement on Monday that Gomez "abused the power given to him by the voters" and that in his actions "he was effectively destroying her dreams of a career in public service".
While they applauded the report, the attorneys said Gomez's conduct "did not occur in a vacuum", calling for immediate steps by Congress to "rein in what the report describes as a 'toxic and predatory culture'".
The committee said in its report on Monday that it did not have enough time "to pursue an adequate House sanction" against Gomez as he is set to leave Congress next month.

title: Black travelers on Route 66 weren't welcome at most gas stations — except this one
summary: Threatt Filling Station in Luther, Okla., was the first Black-owned gas station on Route 66. At a time when Black families needed the Green Book to find places to stay, eat, use the bathroom, it provided fuel and respite.
text:
Black travelers on Route 66 weren't welcome at most gas stations — except this one
During the Jim Crow Era, Black families traveling Route 66, the historic highway that ran more than 2,000 miles from Chicago to Los Angeles, needed to carry food and gas with them. Most restaurants, gas stations and motels wouldn't serve them.
But there was one place they were guaranteed to find respite: a small, family-owned business just east of Oklahoma City that offered fuel, food and a place to stop for the night. The Threatt Filling Station, according to the National Trust for Historic Preservation, was the only known Black-owned and operated gas station along the famous Mother Road.
"Grandpa took care of whatever they needed to have," said Linda Fisher, the granddaughter of the station's founder, Allen Threatt Sr. Her family still owns the station and the 150 acres around it.
"If they didn't have any food, they fed them," she said. "If they needed some kind of shelter or blankets or those types of things, Grandpa and Grandma made sure they got those kinds of things."
Threatt moved from Alabama to the farming community of Luther, Okla., in the early 1900s as part of the Great Migration. His father had been born into slavery, and Threatt and his wife, Alberta, seeking stability and refuge, wanted their own farm.
At the time, Oklahoma was a place where Black migrants could own land and form their own towns. Between 1865 and 1920, Black Americans settled more than 50 "all-Black" municipalities in Oklahoma, the largest number of any state.
But Oklahoma also had its issues — by the time of the Great Depression, many of those all-Black towns had ceased to exist. And there was a rise in "sundown towns": all-white communities that warned non-white people to get out before dark, or they would face violence or police harassment. There was a sundown town on either side of the filling station during the Jim Crow era, Fisher said.
But at the Threatt Filling Station, "everyone was welcome," Fisher said.
The building, which closed to the public in the 1970s, is now on the National Register of Historic Places.
A century of welcome
Allen Threatt Sr. built the original filling station in 1915, when he started to notice people driving by a corner of his property on what was then the Ozark Trail.
In 1926, Route 66 was founded, and the trickle of cars became a steady stream. When the old wooden building burned down, Threatt replaced it with a charming sandstone one, built like a small, welcoming house.
Eventually, the station and the property surrounding it became a community hub. There were dances in the restaurant next door, social club meetings, barbecues. Occasionally, players from the Negro Leagues would have a game on the baseball diamond.
Allen and Alberta Threatt had 11 living children, and a couple of them took over the running of the station in the 1950s.

title: Israeli air strike kills Hamas internal security chief in Gaza
summary: Naeem Abu Nahel, who had been in the post for two months, is among seven Palestinians reportedly killed in Israeli strikes on Tuesday.
text:
Israeli air strike kills Hamas internal security chief in Gaza
- Published
At least seven Palestinians, including a senior Hamas security official, have been killed in Israeli air strikes in the Gaza Strip, health officials and first responders say.
Naeem Abu Nahel, the head of Hamas's internal security service, was targeted in western Gaza City, Gaza's Hamas-run interior ministry said. The 50-year-old had only been in the position since September, when his predecessor was captured in a raid by Israeli special forces.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz announced that Abu Nahel was "eliminated" by the Israeli military.
The six other people were killed in two earlier air strikes elsewhere in Gaza.
Three people, including a teenage boy, were killed in the Wadi Gaza area, south of Gaza City, according to the health officials and first responders. The other three were killed at a police station in the al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Younis, they added.
Gaza's police force, which operates under the interior ministry, said two of its officers were among those who died in the second attack. It also accused Israel of "an ongoing campaign targeting the police apparatus aimed at sowing chaos" in the territory.
The Israeli military said it struck "military operatives" in both areas.
Witnesses said an Israeli drone targeted Naeem Abu Nahel as he was walking on a side street near a tent camp for displaced people in Gaza City.
Several other people were reportedly seriously injured in the strike.
The Israeli military said Abu Nahel had "possessed extensive institutional knowledge" about Hamas's internal security service - which is responsible for enforcing discipline, protecting infrastructure and rooting out informants - and that his death constituted "a blow to the apparatus's management capabilities".
It also alleged that he had advanced attacks on Israeli troops and civilians during the war and that it killed him "to remove the threat he posed".
Gaza's interior ministry said Abu Nahel's killing followed what it described as the internal security service's "important achievements in combating gangs collaborating with the occupation [Israel] and operating in areas under the control of its military".
Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under Hamas's control, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.
At least 1,679 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.
The humanitarian situation also remains dire, with heavy rainfall earlier this month causing flooding and damage to thousands of shelters for displaced families.

A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to Nvidia
Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO of Nvidia earlier this month, after admitting an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy - he was also accused of an affair with an Nvidia executive.
US President Donald Trump says he "made the deal" to encourage Nvidia's board to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO and president.
